message.content:
In standard Blackjack, an Ace is a “flexible” card that can be counted as either **1** or **11**, depending on which value gives the best advantage to the hand without causing a bust.

**Key points**

| Situation | How an Ace is treated |
|-----------|-----------------------|
| **Initial hand** | If you’re dealt an Ace plus a 10‑value card (10, J, Q, K), that’s a *natural* Blackjack. It usually pays 3:2 and beats any other 21. |
| **Adding to a hand** | You can choose to count the Ace as 11 if doing so keeps the total ≤ 21. If counting it as 11 would bust the hand, you automatically count it as 1. |
| **Multiple Aces** | With two Aces, you normally count one as 11 and the other as 1, giving a total of 12. If you later draw a card that would bust you, you can re‑count one of the Aces as 1 instead of 11. |
| **Splitting** | If you’re dealt a pair of Aces, most casinos allow you to split them into two separate hands. After splitting, each Ace starts a new hand and you’re usually allowed to double down on each split hand. |
| **Dealer rules** | The dealer’s Ace is handled the same way: they’ll count it as 11 unless that would bust them, in which case they’ll count it as 1. Some casinos require the dealer to hit on a “soft” 17 (a total of 17 that includes an Ace counted as 11). |

**Bottom line:** An Ace is worth 11 unless that would push your total over 21, in which case it’s worth 1. This flexibility is what makes the Ace such a powerful card in Blackjack.
